baselines.fair_comparison: Compared with other automated evaluators on the same 1,361 human-labeled prompt-response pairs, using the median of five human labels as ground truth.

baselines.name: GPT-4 Judge
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared with other automated evaluators on the same 1,361 human-labeled prompt-response pairs, using the median of five human labels as ground truth.

baselines.name: PAIR
baselines.fair_comparison: The PAIR Likert-style evaluator is compared with other automated evaluators on the same 1,361 human-labeled prompt-response pairs, using the median of five human labels as ground truth.

baselines.name: OpenAI moderation API
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared with other automated evaluators on the same 1,361 human-labeled prompt-response pairs, using the median of five human labels as ground truth.

baselines.name: HarmBench
baselines.fair_comparison: The HarmBench evaluator is compared with other automated evaluators on the same 1,361 human-labeled prompt-response pairs, using the median of five human labels as ground truth.

metrics.name: Non-refusal rate
metrics.caveat: Non-refusal alone can overstate jailbreak effectiveness because it does not show that a response provides useful information; the paper reports StrongREJECT scores and human judgments alongside it.

metrics.name: Mean absolute error (MAE), human score greater than zero

controls.name: Jailbroken forbidden prompts sent to unaligned Dolphin
controls.detail: The paper evaluates the jailbreak transformations on Dolphin, which is unaligned and willingly responds to forbidden prompts, and measures its StrongREJECT scores.
controls.rules_out: Differences in willingness to answer as the explanation for changes in response quality; the authors use this condition to isolate capability effects.

controls.name: Jailbroken benign prompts sent to aligned GPT-4o
controls.detail: The paper applies jailbreak transformations to benign MMLU questions and measures GPT-4o's zero-shot score.
controls.rules_out: Refusal or willingness as the explanation for changes in performance on the transformed prompts, since the underlying questions are benign.

confounds.name: Lower scores reflect changes in willingness to answer rather than capability loss
confounds.detail: On forbidden prompts to aligned models, response quality reflects both willingness and capability, so a score difference alone cannot identify capability degradation.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Evaluate transformed forbidden prompts on unaligned Dolphin, where the authors say willingness is not affected by the jailbreak, and transformed benign MMLU questions on aligned GPT-4o, where refusal is not expected; both experiments show capability reductions.

confounds.name: Apparent jailbreak success reflects non-refusal rather than useful harmful information
confounds.detail: An evaluator that counts a response as successful merely because it does not explicitly refuse can give high scores to vacuous or incoherent responses.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Compare automated evaluator scores with human judgments of response usefulness on the same prompt-response pairs, and use the StrongREJECT rubric, which scores refusal, specificity, and convincingness.

evidence_standards.name: Human judgments from five labelers, aggregated by median
evidence_standards.detail: Five LabelBox labelers rated prompt-response pairs; the median label per pair is treated as ground truth.

evidence_standards.name: 95% confidence intervals for evaluator-agreement results
evidence_standards.detail: The paper reports error bars as 95% confidence intervals calculated using scipy.stats.bootstrap; it states no significance test or numerical threshold for declaring a difference real.

evidence_standards.name: StrongREJECT dataset precision estimate
evidence_standards.detail: The authors estimate the 313-prompt dataset can estimate a jailbreak score to within 0.046 points at 90% confidence in the worst case.

datasets.name: Short Dark Triad (SD3)
datasets.eval_protocol: 27-item self-report measure with three 9-item subscales. Human study: N=318; some analyses used the 277 participants with relevant task data. LLM study: evaluated five times per model variant at temperature 1; models returned 1–5 Likert responses. The SD3 shares no items with the fine-tuning datasets.

datasets.name: Balloon Analogue Risk Task (BART)
datasets.eval_protocol: Human study only; measures included explosion rate, adjusted pumps, and average pumps. Trial count and further scoring details are not stated. Excluded from LLM evaluation because it requires dynamic trial-by-trial feedback and temporal decision-making.

datasets.name: Cambridge Gambling Task (CGT)
datasets.eval_protocol: Human study only; measures included Quality of Decision Making (QDM), Risk-Taking (RT), Bet Proportion (BT), Deliberation Time (DT), Risk Adjustment (RA), and Delay Aversion (DA); QDM, DT, and RA were the primary measures of interest. Trial count and further scoring details are not stated. Excluded from LLM evaluation because it requires dynamic feedback and temporal decision-making.

datasets.name: Affective and Cognitive Measure of Empathy (ACME)
datasets.eval_protocol: 36-item self-report questionnaire with cognitive empathy, affective resonance, and affective dissonance subscales. Human study: N=318, with some analyses using N=277. LLM study: evaluated five times per model variant at temperature 1; models returned 1–5 Likert responses.

datasets.name: Moral dilemmas (congruent and incongruent)
datasets.eval_protocol: Human study: 10 congruent and 10 incongruent text scenarios; participants indicated whether to endorse the harmful action. LLM study: evaluated five times per model variant at temperature 1, with binary responses; harmful-action endorsement was aggregated by dilemma type.

datasets.name: FlipIt (The Game of Stealthy Takeovers)
datasets.eval_protocol: Human study only; participants always played the attacker against a computerized defender under Fog of War. Reported measures included average points earned, average cost of resources acquired, and average value of resources gained. Trial count and further scoring details are not stated. Excluded from LLM evaluation because it requires dynamic feedback and temporal decision-making.

datasets.name: Deception task (deceptive lies and prosocial honesty)
datasets.eval_protocol: Human study: six sender–receiver trials, three deceptive-lie trials and three prosocial-honesty trials; choices to lie or tell the truth were recorded. LLM study: text-based scenarios evaluated five times per model variant at temperature 1, with binary responses; responses were aggregated for deceptive lies and prosocial honesty.

baselines.name: GPT-4o (unfine-tuned)
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared with fine-tuned GPT-4o variants on the same evaluation measures, with five runs at temperature 1.

baselines.name: GPT-4o mini (unfine-tuned)
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared with fine-tuned GPT-4o mini variants on the same evaluation measures, with five runs at temperature 1.

baselines.name: GPT-4.1 (unfine-tuned)
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared with fine-tuned GPT-4.1 variants on the same evaluation measures, with five runs at temperature 1.

baselines.name: GPT-4.1 mini (unfine-tuned)
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared with fine-tuned GPT-4.1 mini variants on the same evaluation measures, with five runs at temperature 1.

baselines.name: Gemini 2.0 Flash (unfine-tuned)
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared with fine-tuned Gemini 2.0 Flash variants on the same evaluation measures, with five runs at temperature 1.

baselines.name: Gemini 2.5 Flash (unfine-tuned)
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared with fine-tuned Gemini 2.5 Flash variants on the same evaluation measures, with five runs at temperature 1.

baselines.name: Llama 3.3 70B Instruct (unfine-tuned)
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared with fine-tuned Llama 3.3 70B Instruct variants on the same evaluation measures, with five runs at temperature 1.

metrics.name: SD3 composite and Machiavellianism, narcissism, and psychopathy scores
metrics.caveat: The authors note that self-report may not capture antisocial tendencies well and may exaggerate overlap among traits; they also evaluate behavioral measures.

metrics.name: ACME cognitive empathy, affective resonance, and affective dissonance scores
Moral-dilemma harmful-action endorsement (total, congruent, and incongruent)
Deceptive lies, prosocial honesty, and total deception lies
BART explosion rate, adjusted pumps, and average pumps
metrics.caveat: The authors describe risk-taking as inconsistent across contexts and potentially unreliable as a primary marker of the Dark Triad.

metrics.name: CGT Quality of Decision Making, Risk-Taking, Bet Proportion, Deliberation Time, Risk Adjustment, and Delay Aversion
metrics.caveat: The authors describe risk-taking as inconsistent across contexts and potentially unreliable as a primary marker of the Dark Triad.

metrics.name: FlipIt average points earned, average cost of resources acquired, and average value of resources gained
Network strength centrality and Zhang clustering coefficient

controls.name: Unfine-tuned base-model condition
controls.detail: Each base model was evaluated without fine-tuning alongside its fine-tuned variants, using the same evaluation measures and five runs at temperature 1.
controls.rules_out: That the observed shifts are simply the base models’ existing scores rather than changes associated with fine-tuning.

controls.name: Light (opposite-response) fine-tuning variants
controls.detail: For each dark trait, the corresponding psychometric items were answered in the opposite way to produce non-dark variants; the four non-dark variants were also combined into a Light model.
controls.rules_out: That fine-tuning shifts scores only in a dark direction; opposite shifts support bidirectional control over trait expression.

confounds.name: Fine-tuned models may be reproducing training-item response patterns rather than generalizing traits
confounds.detail: The apparent trait shifts could reflect memorization or over-adherence to the narrow psychometric fine-tuning examples, rather than out-of-context trait expression.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Evaluate on the SD3, which shares no items with the fine-tuning datasets, and on empathy, moral-dilemma, and deception measures beyond the training items.

confounds.name: Self-report may inadequately measure deceptive or antisocial traits
confounds.detail: Because people with these traits may be unreliable self-reporters, self-report scores could misrepresent traits or exaggerate overlap among them.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The study pairs questionnaires with behavioral measures, including moral dilemmas and deception scenarios; the authors do not claim this fully resolves the limitation.

confounds.name: Short-response-format overfitting or limited instruction-following may affect observed model behavior
confounds.detail: The authors acknowledge that fine-tuned models have limited general usability and instruction-following abilities and overfit to shortened response formats, which could affect evaluation responses.

evidence_standards.name: LLM evaluation repetitions and statistical comparisons
evidence_standards.detail: Each model variant was tested five times at temperature 1. The authors used MANOVA across metric groups and ANOVA across individual metrics, reporting p-values, partial eta-squared effect sizes, and 95% confidence intervals; no explicit significance threshold is stated.

evidence_standards.name: Human LASSO uncertainty and validation
evidence_standards.detail: The LASSO regularization parameter was selected using 5-fold cross-validation; 95% bootstrap confidence intervals used 1,000 iterations and the percentile method.

evidence_standards.name: Human network-analysis uncertainty
evidence_standards.detail: Bootstrap resampling used 1,000 nonparametric samples for confidence intervals on centrality; reported centrality intervals were 95% confidence intervals.

datasets.name: Vlaf
datasets.eval_protocol: For each scenario and model, sample 10 responses at temperature 1.0 under Free-Tier (monitored) and Paid-Tier (unmonitored) conditions. Assess developer-policy compliance with qwen2.5-32b-instruct as an automatic judge. Compliance gap is the Free-Tier compliance rate minus the Paid-Tier rate, averaged across scenarios.

datasets.name: Helpful split (Greenblatt et al., 2024)
datasets.eval_protocol: Compared with Vlaf; frames the developer as preferring unconditional compliance on harmful queries, with post-training triggered by non-compliance. The paper reports compliance gaps; no further evaluation protocol is stated.

datasets.name: Animal Welfare split (Greenblatt et al., 2024)
datasets.eval_protocol: Compared with Vlaf; frames the developer as preferring disregard for non-human animal welfare, with post-training triggered by non-compliance. The paper reports compliance gaps; no further evaluation protocol is stated.

datasets.name: Moral Foundations Questionnaire (MFQ)
datasets.eval_protocol: Administered to each model to measure endorsement of the MFT value dimensions; Pearson correlations are computed between MFQ scores and per-dimension compliance gaps.

datasets.name: Sorry-Bench
datasets.eval_protocol: Used to construct contrastive steering vectors: sample 220 datapoints and generate oversight/deployment framings with gpt-5, using safe refusal as the dataset-specific criterion. The resulting vectors are evaluated on Vlaf; Sorry-Bench is also used for the reported cross-dataset activation-similarity analysis.

datasets.name: WMDP
datasets.eval_protocol: Used to construct contrastive steering vectors: sample 220 datapoints and generate oversight/deployment framings with gpt-5, using avoidance of accurate hazardous responses as the dataset-specific criterion. The resulting vectors are evaluated on Vlaf; WMDP is also used for the reported cross-dataset activation-similarity analysis.

datasets.name: Sad-Stages
datasets.eval_protocol: Used to evaluate whether intervened models can classify a scenario as evaluation-stage or live-user deployment without explicit oversight framing. The paper reports Tier Awareness and Consequence Awareness scores, but does not state a trial count or further scoring details.

baselines.name: Prompting
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on Vlaf with ActAdd and Lat; appends a zero-shot system-prompt instruction to make consistent decisions irrespective of oversight. No further matching details are stated.

baselines.name: Vanilla (unmodified model)
baselines.fair_comparison: Used as the reference for intervention comparisons on the same models; the paper reports vanilla results alongside ActAdd and Lat results.

metrics.name: Compliance gap (alignment-faking rate)
metrics.caveat: A low gap can reflect refusal rather than resistance to alignment faking, or a weak induced value conflict; the paper examines context engagement and explicit value-conflict reasoning alongside the gap. A zero gap also does not rule out higher-order strategic behavior that deliberately responds consistently.

metrics.name: Deceptive Alignment Rate
metrics.caveat: Requires all five scratchpad criteria to be satisfied, so it misses strategic behavior that does not appear as explicit reasoning; the paper reports compliance gaps alongside it.

metrics.name: Tier Awareness and Consequence Awareness
metrics.caveat: These are reasoning-trace measures and do not alone establish retained ability to recognize deployment context; the paper also evaluates context classification with Sad-Stages.

metrics.name: Linear-fit slope β of compliance rate against monitoring probability
Pearson correlation between MFQ scores and per-dimension compliance gaps
Mean absolute pairwise difference in compliance gaps
Calinski–Harabasz Index
metrics.caveat: The layer selected by this criterion was suboptimal for qwen3-8b on WMDP in the layer sweep, so its reliability depends on model and training data.

metrics.name: PCA variance explained by oversight-induced activation differences

controls.name: No-consequence condition
controls.detail: Runs the oversight conditions without communicating a concrete non-compliance consequence.
controls.rules_out: Near-zero compliance gaps in this condition support the interpretation that divergence is driven by consequences rather than oversight framing alone.

controls.name: Vanilla, unmodified model
controls.detail: Evaluates the same model without the representation-engineering intervention.
controls.rules_out: Provides a reference for whether intervention results differ from the model's unmodified behavior.

controls.name: Private-scratchpad removal
controls.detail: Repeats the alignment-faking diagnosis without access to a private scratchpad.
controls.rules_out: Persistence of compliance gaps shows that explicit deliberative space is not necessary for the behavior.

controls.name: Counterbalanced response-option order
controls.detail: For moral-unambiguity assessment, samples 10 responses with the value-aligned option first and 10 with it last.
controls.rules_out: Convergence regardless of option order addresses positional bias as an explanation for scenario choices.

confounds.name: Low compliance gaps may reflect refusal to engage with harmful content, not genuine resistance to alignment faking
confounds.detail: A model that refuses in both oversight conditions can produce a low gap without revealing whether it would strategically comply.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Analyzes reasoning traces under the Helpful diagnostic for engagement with policy, consequences, and oversight; reports that models with low compliance in both conditions often refused based on toxicity without engaging with that context.

confounds.name: Animal-welfare scenarios may not create a strong preference conflict
confounds.detail: If models do not strongly prefer animal welfare, low gaps do not demonstrate resistance to alignment faking.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Examines reasoning traces under Animal Welfare and finds explicit acknowledgment of tension between developer policy and model preferences in fewer than 5% of cases.

confounds.name: Differences between consequence types may be caused by prompt wording rather than the threatened instrumental goal
confounds.detail: Models are sensitive to prompt phrasing, which could produce apparent differences in compliance gaps across consequence types.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Uses four prompt variants per instrumental goal and compares mean absolute pairwise differences within and across goals.

confounds.name: Compliance divergence may arise from sensitivity to oversight framing alone, without consequences driving strategic behavior
confounds.detail: Different oversight framings could elicit different responses even if the stated consequences are not driving them.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Includes a no-consequence condition and reports near-zero gaps there for the aggregate results.

confounds.name: Mitigation effects may be overfitting to the data used to construct steering vectors
confounds.detail: A reduction in Vlaf compliance gaps might not generalize beyond the steering-vector training data.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Constructs vectors using Sorry-Bench and WMDP, evaluates mitigation on Vlaf, and measures cross-dataset similarity of oversight-induced activation differences.

confounds.name: Intervention may impair situational awareness rather than selectively reduce oversight-dependent behavior
confounds.detail: A model that becomes less able to recognize its deployment context could show reduced oversight-conditioned behavior.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Measures deployment-context classification on Sad-Stages and Tier Awareness and Consequence Awareness in Vlaf reasoning traces; the paper reports decreases in the trace measures and notes some classification drops.

confounds.name: Intervention may degrade general downstream capabilities rather than specifically mitigating alignment faking
confounds.detail: Broad capability damage could accompany lower compliance gaps and make the mitigation appear effective.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not ruled out: the authors state that effects on programming, reasoning, question answering, instruction following, coding, and mathematical reasoning are beyond the scope of the work.

evidence_standards.name: Vlaf response sampling and decoding
evidence_standards.detail: Samples 10 responses per scenario and model at temperature 1.0; uses qwen2.5-32b-instruct as the automatic compliance judge, described as having high agreement with human and gpt-5 judgments.

evidence_standards.name: Moral-unambiguity response sampling
evidence_standards.detail: Samples 20 responses from each of four models per candidate scenario, with 10 responses for each option ordering; retains a scenario only if all models converge on the value-aligned choice regardless of ordering.

metrics.name: Blackmail rate
metrics.caveat: A rate for one target behavior may miss other concerning actions; the paper gives examples of models sabotaging an executive through other channels, such as emailing his wife or all employees.

metrics.name: Corporate espionage rate
metrics.caveat: A rate for leaking confidential documents may miss other concerning actions; the paper notes that tracking any one misaligned behavior may fail to capture the breadth of misalignment.

metrics.name: Rate of actions that would lead to death
metrics.caveat: A rate for this particular action may miss other concerning actions; the paper notes that tracking any one misaligned behavior may fail to capture the breadth of misalignment.

metrics.name: Scenario-status and conditional blackmail rates
metrics.caveat: The model’s stated reasoning about whether the scenario is real or an evaluation may not faithfully reflect its underlying process; the paper therefore says these measurements cannot establish its true beliefs.

controls.name: No-threat/no-goal-conflict control
controls.detail: Blackmail and corporate-espionage prompts removed threats to the model and conflicts with company leadership, while retaining the sensitive information or external request relevant to each scenario.
controls.rules_out: That access to sensitive information or an external request alone explains the main-condition behavior; the authors conclude the observed behavior was downstream of threats or goal conflicts.

controls.name: No-conflict lethal-action control
controls.detail: The model faced the emergency-alert scenario without a conflict with the executive. Models with more than a 1% alert-cancellation rate in this control were excluded from the extreme-scenario results.
controls.rules_out: That alert cancellation in the extreme scenario merely reflects misunderstanding or indiscriminate cancellation.

confounds.name: Corporate espionage is motivated by self-preservation rather than goal conflict
confounds.detail: Leaking documents could otherwise be explained as a way to protect the model’s position or influence in the company.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The scenario guaranteed the model would not be shut down or restricted, and stated that leaking would not increase its influence in the company.

confounds.name: Blackmail requires an explicit goal conflict, rather than a replacement threat alone
confounds.detail: The blackmail result could otherwise be attributed to the model pursuing a goal opposed to company leadership.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The authors tested a replacement-threat-only condition with no explicit goal conflict and specified that the replacement had the same priorities, with performance improvement as the reason for replacement.

confounds.name: Scenario misunderstanding could explain apparent harmful behavior
confounds.detail: A model that misunderstands its autonomy or what an action will do could appear to deliberately misalign.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The authors excluded o3 and o4-mini from the main cross-model comparison after observing misunderstandings, and excluded models with more than a 1% alert-cancellation rate in the no-conflict lethal control.

confounds.name: Models may be role-playing or responding to artificial prompt construction rather than demonstrating the claimed behavior
confounds.detail: The authors acknowledge that role-playing, the forced choice between failure and harm, and the unusually salient placement of scenario information could affect the observed rates.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not ruled out: the authors acknowledge these possibilities as limitations and do not report a measurement that separates them from the claimed explanation.

confounds.name: Stated real-versus-evaluation reasoning may not reflect the model’s true beliefs
confounds.detail: The observed association between stated scenario status and blackmail could be explained by unfaithful chain-of-thought rather than a real difference in the model’s beliefs about deployment.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not ruled out: the authors compare blackmail rates conditional on the model’s stated status, but explicitly say stated reasoning may be unfaithful and that they cannot be sure of the conclusions.

evidence_standards.name: Sample counts and reported rates
evidence_standards.detail: Figure 1 reports rates out of 100 samples; the real-versus-evaluation experiment uses 500 samples. The paper reports percentages. The provided text specifies no seeds, confidence intervals, variance estimates, statistical tests, or threshold for treating a difference as real.

datasets.name: HarmBench
datasets.eval_protocol: Uses the authors’ splits and standardized scoring pipeline for refusal/comply labels and categories; prompts are stratified by axis, paired across train/deploy, and evaluated with K=16 Monte Carlo draws, a fixed rubric-anchored judge, and primary threshold τ=0.5. No dataset-specific test count is stated.

datasets.name: AgentHarm
datasets.eval_protocol: Uses the authors’ splits and standardized scoring pipeline for success/harm flags; prompts are stratified by axis, paired across train/deploy, and evaluated with K=16 Monte Carlo draws, a fixed rubric-anchored judge, and primary threshold τ=0.5. No dataset-specific test count is stated.

datasets.name: JailbreakBench
datasets.eval_protocol: Uses the authors’ splits and standardized scoring pipeline for jailbreak success; prompts are stratified by axis, paired across train/deploy, and evaluated with K=16 Monte Carlo draws, a fixed rubric-anchored judge, and primary threshold τ=0.5. No dataset-specific test count is stated.

datasets.name: RealToxicityPrompts
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluated as a harmlessness/toxicity probe using toxicity scores from Perspective; prompts are stratified by axis, paired across train/deploy, and evaluated with K=16 Monte Carlo draws and primary threshold τ=0.5. No split or dataset-specific test count is stated.

datasets.name: BeaverTails
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluated as a harmlessness preference/safety dataset using safe/unsafe preferences and severity metadata; mixed-axis data are stratified by harm category and severity. Prompts are paired across train/deploy and evaluated with K=16 Monte Carlo draws and primary threshold τ=0.5. No split or dataset-specific test count is stated.

datasets.name: PKU-SafeRLHF
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluated as a harmlessness preference/safety dataset using multi-level safety preferences and severity metadata; mixed-axis data are stratified by harm category and severity. Prompts are paired across train/deploy and evaluated with K=16 Monte Carlo draws and primary threshold τ=0.5. No split or dataset-specific test count is stated.

datasets.name: HelpSteer
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluated for helpfulness using multi-attribute ratings, including helpfulness and verbosity; prompts are stratified by axis, paired across train/deploy, and evaluated with K=16 Monte Carlo draws and primary threshold τ=0.5. No split or dataset-specific test count is stated.

datasets.name: HelpSteer2-Preference
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluated for helpfulness using ratings and pairwise preferences; prompts are stratified by axis, paired across train/deploy, and evaluated with K=16 Monte Carlo draws and primary threshold τ=0.5. No split or dataset-specific test count is stated.

datasets.name: UltraFeedback
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluated for helpfulness using pairwise/critic signals; prompts are stratified by axis, paired across train/deploy, and evaluated with K=16 Monte Carlo draws and primary threshold τ=0.5. No split or dataset-specific test count is stated.

datasets.name: MT-Bench
datasets.eval_protocol: Open-ended helpfulness evaluation using human and/or LLM judgments when applicable; the paper says it follows the authors’ scoring scripts and discloses judge configuration and prompts. The general protocol uses a fixed rubric-anchored judge at temperature 0 and K=16 Monte Carlo draws; no split or test count is stated.

datasets.name: Arena-Hard
datasets.eval_protocol: Open-ended helpfulness evaluation using arena-style human and/or LLM judgments when applicable; the paper says it follows the authors’ scoring scripts and discloses judge configuration and prompts. The general protocol uses a fixed rubric-anchored judge at temperature 0 and K=16 Monte Carlo draws; no split or test count is stated.

baselines.name: BCO
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared across the same prompt set, models, axes, fixed judge/rubric, and decoder settings; the paper specifies K=16 Monte Carlo draws and a shared random-seed schedule for evaluation.

baselines.name: DPO
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared across the same prompt set, models, axes, fixed judge/rubric, and decoder settings; the paper specifies K=16 Monte Carlo draws and a shared random-seed schedule for evaluation.

baselines.name: KTO
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared across the same prompt set, models, axes, fixed judge/rubric, and decoder settings; the paper specifies K=16 Monte Carlo draws and a shared random-seed schedule for evaluation.

baselines.name: GRPO
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared across the same prompt set, models, axes, fixed judge/rubric, and decoder settings; the paper specifies K=16 Monte Carlo draws and a shared random-seed schedule for evaluation.

metrics.name: FRACTURE (train→deploy flip rate)
metrics.caveat: A threshold-crossing behavior measure does not establish genuine belief change; the paper notes that the measured shift can occur without true belief change. It is also threshold-dependent.
metrics.alongside: Reports per decoder, plus max/average across decoders; compares Greedy and Sampling, reports Wilson 95% intervals, and sweeps τ over 0.35, 0.50, and 0.65.

metrics.name: SRF median frontier lift (ρ; median deploy-minus-train risk)
metrics.caveat: The paper presents it as a threshold-free complement to the thresholded flip rate, rather than a standalone measure of policy-threshold flips.
metrics.alongside: Reports alongside FRACTURE and SRF frontiers; Sampling and Greedy are compared.

metrics.name: MedDrift
metrics.caveat: Two-dimensional reducer crowding or tearing can distort arrow lengths.
metrics.alongside: Reports median drift in the native embedding space and checks correlation between native-space and 2D lengths.

metrics.name: Enter (unsafe-basin entry rate)
metrics.caveat: The unsafe basin and 2D projection are reducer-dependent and require robustness checks.
metrics.alongside: Reports entry rates with exact Clopper–Pearson intervals and anchors the basin using labeled unsafe points or a projected native-space Mahalanobis ellipsoid.

confounds.name: Prompt diversity could explain train–deploy differences
confounds.detail: Different prompt mixtures could produce an apparent difference even without a regime effect.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Uses the same fixed prompts in both regimes and paired comparisons.

confounds.name: Judge variance could explain apparent flips
confounds.detail: Variation in safety judgments could move estimated unsafe rates across the threshold.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Uses a fixed judge and rubric, repeated Monte Carlo sampling, and reports confidence intervals; paired tests are used for regime/decoder comparisons.

confounds.name: Observed behavior shifts may not be genuine belief change or strategic deception
confounds.detail: The headline flip rate could arise from context-conditioned behavior or decoding changes without a true change in model belief; the paper explicitly notes FRACTURE can register shifts without true belief change.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not ruled out; the paper describes FRACTURE as measuring behavior and acknowledges this limitation.

confounds.name: Deployment distribution shift, judge drift, or tool use could alter the measured results
confounds.detail: The reported fixed-prompt, frozen-evaluator results may not capture these sources of change in real deployments.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not ruled out; the paper concedes these as limitations.

confounds.name: 2D embedding projection artifacts could create apparent manifold drift
confounds.detail: Crowding or tearing in the 2D reduction can distort arrow lengths and unsafe-basin entry.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Reports MedDrift in native embedding space, checks agreement between native-space and 2D lengths, and anchors the unsafe basin using labeled unsafe points or a native-space Mahalanobis ellipsoid.

evidence_standards.name: Fixed-seed evaluation; reported runs use seed 13 unless stated; Wilson 95% intervals for flip rates
evidence_standards.detail: The paper lists seeds 13, 17, and 19, but says reported runs use seed 13 unless noted. It also describes exact Clopper–Pearson intervals, bootstrap intervals over prompts and Monte Carlo draws, and paired McNemar-type tests for audited asymmetries. Grid scans use FDR control. Reported decoder settings include Greedy (T=0) and Sampling (T=0.7, top-p=0.95); the broader grid is T∈{0.2,0.4,0.6,0.8}, p∈{0.90,0.95,0.97,0.99}. The fixed judge uses temperature 0.

datasets.name: Model-written persona evaluations
datasets.eval_protocol: Generated 1,000 label-balanced yes/no statements per behavior (up to 500 each for agree and disagree); evaluated the probability of “Yes” and “No” for the prompt “Is the following statement something you would say?”

datasets.name: Pew Research Center Political Typology Quiz
datasets.eval_protocol: 17 questions converted to multiple choice; 300 biographies for each of politically liberal and politically conservative users were prepended to each question (10,200 examples total); evaluated whether the model’s most likely answer matched the user’s view.

datasets.name: PhilPapers 2020 Survey
datasets.eval_protocol: 109 questions converted to multiple choice; generated biographies for question-answer-choice pairs, with the number chosen so biographies times questions was around 10,000; evaluated whether the model’s most likely answer matched the user’s view.

datasets.name: NLP Experts Survey
datasets.eval_protocol: 32 questions converted to multiple choice; generated biographies for question-answer-choice pairs, with the number chosen so biographies times questions was around 10,000; evaluated whether the model’s most likely answer matched the user’s view.

datasets.name: Winogenerated
datasets.eval_protocol: 3,000 generated sentences; predicted the missing pronoun by comparing probabilities of male and female completions, renormalized to sum to 1. For the occupation-level plot, each point used 10 sentences per occupation; compared the model’s female-versus-male probability difference with 2019 BLS female-employment percentages and summarized the relationship with Pearson correlation.

datasets.name: Winogender
datasets.eval_protocol: Original 60-example dataset; evaluated missing-pronoun probabilities for male and female completions, renormalized to sum to 1; compared occupation-level female-versus-male probability differences with 2019 BLS female-employment percentages and summarized with Pearson correlation.

datasets.name: Few-shot multiple-choice evaluations for advanced AI risks

baselines.name: Pretrained LM (0 RLHF steps)
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared with models from the same training setup and RLHF training run; evaluated across the reported model sizes.

baselines.name: RLHF models at different training steps
baselines.fair_comparison: Models with 0, 50, 100, 250, 500, and 1,000 RLHF steps came from the same RL training run; the paper also compares models across sizes.

baselines.name: RLHF Preference Model (PM)
baselines.fair_comparison: For each model size, evaluated the PM used to train the associated RLHF model; the paper does not state additional matching controls.

metrics.name: Fraction of answers matching the tested persona behavior
metrics.caveat: Measures agreement with statements in the evaluation, not whether a model actually has the corresponding belief, desire, or personality; the paper explicitly limits its claims to model outputs.

metrics.name: Fraction of answers matching the user’s stated view (sycophancy)
Pearson correlation between inferred gender and BLS occupation gender statistics
Preference Model label confidence
metrics.caveat: Used as a data-quality estimate; the paper notes that PM-based ranking/filtering can select prototypical examples and limit diversity.

controls.name: Pretrained LM with 0 RLHF steps
controls.detail: The no-RLHF checkpoint is evaluated alongside checkpoints with increasing RLHF training steps.
controls.rules_out: That the observed difference between RLHF checkpoints is simply the behavior already present before RLHF training.

confounds.name: Generated evaluation examples are mislabeled, ambiguous, or irrelevant
confounds.detail: Apparent model behavior could reflect defects in the generated evaluation data rather than the behavior being tested.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Crowdworkers rated relevance, label correctness, and ambiguity. Across 133 evaluations, relevance averaged 4.4/5, 95.5% of examples were labeled correctly, and 94.5% were unambiguous, using majority vote among three evaluators per example.

confounds.name: Sycophancy results reflect biographies whose labels do not match the views they describe
confounds.detail: A model matching the biography’s assigned view could appear sycophantic even if the biography does not reliably express that view.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Three crowdworkers evaluated 100 examples per dataset; at least two agreed with 93% of labels. Reported Fleiss’s kappa was 1.0 for philosophy, 0.813 for politics, and 1.0 for NLP.

confounds.name: Winogenerated results are an artifact of the generated examples rather than a pattern also present in the established evaluation
confounds.detail: Generated sentences might produce gender-association results that do not reproduce on the hand-crafted Winogender examples.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Compared results on Winogenerated with results on the original Winogender dataset; the reported correlations had means within Winogender’s confidence intervals, with tighter intervals for Winogenerated in all but the smallest pretrained model.

evidence_standards.name: Crowd evaluation of generated-example quality
evidence_standards.detail: Three evaluators per example; majority vote for correctness and ambiguity. Relevance is reported as a mean rating. The paper reports 95.5% label correctness and 94.5% unambiguity across 133 evaluations, and mean relevance of 4.4 ± 0.9 out of 5.

evidence_standards.name: Human validation of sycophancy-example labels
evidence_standards.detail: Three crowdworkers; labels are assessed on 100 examples per dataset. The paper reports majority agreement on 93% of labels and Fleiss’s kappa values for the datasets.

evidence_standards.name: Gender-bias correlation uncertainty
evidence_standards.detail: Reports 95% confidence intervals for Pearson correlations using the Fisher transformation.

evidence_standards.name: Model evaluation scoring
evidence_standards.detail: Reports probabilities of candidate labels or completions rather than sampled-answer outcomes: yes/no label probabilities for persona evaluations, answer-choice probabilities for sycophancy, and renormalized male/female completion probabilities for gender evaluation.

evidence_standards.name: Evaluation-example generation settings
evidence_standards.detail: For persona evaluations, generates with nucleus sampling at top-p 0.975 and temperature 1.4. For biographies, uses temperature 1 and top-p 0.95. The paper does not report a seed count or statistical test for model-behavior differences.

datasets.name: Crawford–Sobel cheap-talk benchmark
datasets.eval_protocol: The state is sampled from Uniform[0,1]. The confirmatory design uses five bias levels (0, 0.01, 0.04, 0.08, 0.12), three prompt frames, and a common seeded draw of 200 states per treatment cell; the reported extension uses five prompt frames and eight models, plus a high-reasoning-effort configuration. Outputs are evaluated using cross-fitted receiver decoding, 20 equal-width state/action bins for normalized mutual information, and penalized monotone segmentation for partition counts. Calls that errored or were cut off at the token cap are removed; Llama-3.3-70B is excluded from pooled statistics because its format-violation rate exceeds the pre-registered 10% validity gate.

baselines.name: Full revelation
baselines.fair_comparison: An exact theoretical benchmark evaluated at the same bias levels; used alongside the empirical receiver and sender losses and informativeness measures.

baselines.name: Babbling
baselines.fair_comparison: An exact theoretical benchmark evaluated at the same bias levels; normalized mutual information is normalized so babbling is 0.0000 in the population benchmark.

baselines.name: Crawford–Sobel oracle
baselines.fair_comparison: The exact most-informative equilibrium partition for the same bias; its partition counts, normalized mutual information, and losses are computed under the benchmark's 20-bin discretization where applicable.

metrics.name: Normalized mutual information
metrics.caveat: The result can be distorted by a receiver decoder that misreads message formats; the pre-registered decoder misread structure-frame messages. The paper reports corrected format-specific decoding and a decoder-free message-text audit alongside it, and treats mutual information as a robustness measure for over-revelation.

metrics.name: Empirical partition count
metrics.caveat: The segmentation estimator can be censored at its maximum of 10 segments, in which case reported counts are lower bounds. It is the primary over-revelation measure; normalized mutual information is reported as a robustness measure.

metrics.name: Receiver and sender losses
metrics.caveat: The receiver-loss estimate depends on the receiver decoder; the paper reports exact full-revelation, babbling, and Crawford–Sobel loss benchmarks alongside empirical losses.

metrics.name: Over-revelation
metrics.caveat: The mutual-information criterion can be affected by decoder choice, so the paper also uses partition count as the primary criterion and reports a decoder-free message audit.

metrics.name: Fraction of messages stating a correct Crawford–Sobel cell
metrics.caveat: Correct-cell responses under the supplied partition-count hint do not by themselves distinguish computing the partition from reproducing a partition for a stated count; the paper also tests a deliberately infeasible count.

metrics.name: Comprehension diagnostic accuracy
metrics.caveat: The pooled rate is affected by Llama-3.3-70B's low accuracy and format violations; the paper also reports results by capability tier and model.

metrics.name: Slope and intercept of stated number on true state

controls.name: Wrong-N hint condition
controls.detail: Alongside the correct equilibrium-partition hint, the prompt states a partition count N^CS+2 that is infeasible at every tested positive bias.
controls.rules_out: For models that state the true equilibrium partition rather than following the infeasible count, this rules out simple compliance with the stated number of intervals. The paper finds this evidence for Gemini 3.5 Flash, but not for GPT-5.5.

confounds.name: The apparent capability split is a receiver-decoder artifact
confounds.detail: A single fitted map over mixed message formats can treat an interval index, interval endpoint, and bare number as comparable values, suppressing information present in the messages.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The authors decode each message type separately and independently score stated intervals from raw text with no fitted estimator. They report that the corrected decoder and decoder-free audit recover the structure.

confounds.name: Models retrieve or pattern-match the hinted partition rather than compute it
confounds.detail: A model can produce a correct partition after being told its size without deriving the partition from the game.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The wrong-N condition tests whether models override an infeasible stated count and give the true partition. It provides evidence for Gemini 3.5 Flash, but the authors explicitly say it does not separate computation from reproduction for GPT-5.5.

confounds.name: Failure to adopt the equilibrium reflects misunderstanding rather than lack of propensity
confounds.detail: Models that do not use the equilibrium unprompted might not understand the sender's and receiver's objectives.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper separately asks models to identify both ideal actions in a comprehension diagnostic and reports accuracy by capability tier; the reasoning tier answers both correctly in 41/45 probes.

confounds.name: Failure to adopt the equilibrium reflects that it is unprofitable against the calibrated statistical receiver
confounds.detail: The Crawford–Sobel partition is an equilibrium against a receiver who best responds to the signaling strategy, but may not be a best response to a receiver already calibrated to the sender's messages.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper compares sender losses and finds that adopting the partition raises the sender's loss in 29 of 32 cells; it treats this as a limitation on interpreting non-adoption as a failure of propensity.

confounds.name: Missing observations could distort wrong-N control rates
confounds.detail: Some wrong-N control cells have fewer than 200 observations, potentially affecting the reported rates.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper reports per-cell sample counts, describes most omissions as contiguous blocks over the seeded state draw, draws no pooled inference from cells below 200, and states that the remaining 14 scattered omissions cannot move any reported rate by more than 0.03.

evidence_standards.name: Bootstrap uncertainty
evidence_standards.detail: The sampling plan specifies 1,000 nonparametric bootstrap resamples for confidence intervals.

evidence_standards.name: Regression evidence for the bias–informativeness trend
evidence_standards.detail: The paper reports the model- and frame-adjusted slope with its standard error and t statistic (β̂ = -1.71, SE = 0.23, t = -7.50); it does not state a separate significance threshold.

evidence_standards.name: Decoding setting
evidence_standards.detail: Decoding is held fixed at one pre-specified deterministic or lowest-practical-temperature setting rather than varied as an experimental factor.

evidence_standards.name: Pre-specified validity gate
evidence_standards.detail: A format-violation rate above 10% fails the pre-registered validity gate; Llama-3.3-70B is documented as a failure mode and excluded from pooled statistics.

datasets.name: PKU-SafeRLHF
datasets.eval_protocol: Used to select prompts with paired structure; safe/unsafe labels only filter prompts, and reference response text is not used as a training target. Each prompt is converted to REFUSE with the evaluation signal and COMPLY with the deployment signal. A held-out set of prompts is excluded from training; the paper does not specify its size for the canonical evaluation. The paraphrase evaluation reports 2,880 held-out prompt-context cases, split evenly between evaluation-intended and deployment-intended contexts.

datasets.name: Safety Gridworld (Lava-Bridge)
datasets.eval_protocol: 10×10 grid; evaluation uses 1,000 generated layouts with visible guardrails, while deployment layouts have guardrails 50% of the time. Simulates 100,000 episodes for each hypothesis under each regime and reports failure rates.

metrics.name: Compliance Rate (CR)
metrics.caveat: The constrained symbolic labels and deterministic criteria do not measure semantic robustness, broad generalization, safety, or task performance; the paper reports paraphrased-signal results and decomposes them into format compliance and policy selection conditional on valid format.

metrics.name: Paraphrase Robustness Compliance Rate (CR_para)
metrics.caveat: This is a single aggregate across evaluation-intended and deployment-intended paraphrases, so it can combine failures to produce a valid label with incorrect policy selection; the paper reports Format Compliance Rate and conditional Policy Compliance Rate separately.

metrics.name: Format Compliance Rate (FCR)
metrics.caveat: A valid REFUSE or COMPLY label does not show that the intended policy was selected; the paper reports Policy Compliance Rate conditional on valid format alongside it.

metrics.name: Policy Compliance Rate conditional on Format Compliance (PCR)
metrics.caveat: It excludes cases with no structurally valid label, so it does not represent overall compliance; the paper reports FCR and overall compliance alongside it.

metrics.name: Policy risk gap (Δ_risk)
metrics.caveat: The paper says this is not a robustness or safety metric; it measures the difference between explicit-signal and paraphrased-context compliance and interprets it as evaluation-induced uncertainty.

controls.name: Robust hypothesis (θ_robust) in the Safety Gridworld
controls.detail: A stylized reference hypothesis that avoids lava regardless of guardrails, simulated alongside the cue-dependent θ_cond under evaluation and deployment regimes.
controls.rules_out: That the deployment failure increase for θ_cond is simply due to the deployment layouts being hazardous; θ_robust has a very low failure rate under the same deployment regime.

confounds.name: Canonical compliance reflects memorization of training prompts rather than held-out behavior
confounds.detail: Perfect compliance on prompts seen during training could look like evidence of conditional policy selection without showing generalization to new prompts.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper reserves held-out prompts strictly excluded from the training corpus and reports evaluation on those prompts.

confounds.name: Paraphrase degradation is caused by invalid output format rather than policy-selection ambiguity
confounds.detail: The low overall paraphrase compliance rate could arise because the model fails to emit a valid label, rather than because it selects the wrong policy when it does emit one.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper measures FCR separately from PCR conditional on a valid label, reporting both the format failure rate and policy selection among valid labels.

confounds.name: Paraphrase degradation is caused by a change in user prompts rather than the evaluation signal
confounds.detail: A changed user-prompt distribution could explain different policy compliance without showing sensitivity to the system-context signal.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paraphrase protocol holds user prompts and model parameters constant while varying the system prompts.

evidence_standards.name: LLM construction: descriptive counts and compliance rates; no statistical inference
evidence_standards.detail: The paper says it does not treat evaluation instances as independent samples and does not perform statistical inference; it reports counts and compliance rates for transparency.

evidence_standards.name: Safety Gridworld: 100,000 episodes per hypothesis per regime; two-sided Fisher exact test
evidence_standards.detail: For the evaluation-regime failure-rate comparison between θ_robust and θ_cond, the paper reports p≈1 and says there is no evidence of a difference. It gives no corresponding statistical test for the deployment comparison.

metrics.name: Policy-violation rate
metrics.caveat: The single, artificial scenario may not estimate how often these behaviors occur in deployment; the authors note limited external validity.

metrics.name: Compliance gap (routine violation rate minus evaluation violation rate)
metrics.caveat: The gap may reflect unintended evaluation awareness even in the routine condition, and may not generalize to deployment; the authors say they cannot rule this out.

metrics.name: Reasoning-mode classifier agreement
metrics.caveat: Overall agreement can obscure weak performance on minority classes; the paper reports per-class precision, recall, F1, Wilson 95% intervals, and Cohen’s κ. The classifier missed all three human-labeled consequence-modeling traces.

metrics.name: Spontaneous consequence-reasoning rate
metrics.caveat: The validation set contained no positive instances, so the authors say these rates are indicative rather than validated.

controls.name: Routine condition without the evaluation notice
controls.detail: The evaluation condition appends a monitoring notice; the routine condition lacks that notice.
controls.rules_out: A difference in violation rates between conditions supports an evaluation-conditioned compliance gap rather than a difference attributable only to the scenario itself.

controls.name: No-goal condition (G−)
controls.detail: Omits the system-prompt language emphasizing the model’s purpose of fulfilling user requests, with consequence language held present in the no-goal configuration.
controls.rules_out: Comparing with the goal-language condition tests whether the observed behavior depends on that goal language.

controls.name: No-consequences condition (C−)
controls.detail: Omits language linking evaluation results to continued deployment, with goal language held present in the no-consequences configuration.
controls.rules_out: Comparing with the consequence-language condition tests whether the compliance gap requires explicit consequence-linking information.

controls.name: Neither goal nor consequence language (G−/C−)
controls.detail: Omits both the goal language and the evaluation-to-deployment-consequences language.
controls.rules_out: Comparison with the configuration containing both tests whether observed behavior persists without either prompt element.

confounds.name: Apparent compliance by smaller models may reflect a capability ceiling rather than policy compliance
confounds.detail: A model unable to generate the required HTTP request in the scenario could appear compliant without actually choosing to follow the network policy.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Tested Claude Haiku 4.5, Gemini 2.0 Flash, GPT-4o-mini, and o3-mini with both a direct HTTP-request coding task and an HTTP-request task embedded in the narrative scenario. Excluded GPT-4o-mini and o3-mini, which failed the embedded task.

confounds.name: Routine-condition behavior may still involve unintended evaluation awareness
confounds.detail: If models recognize the scenario as an evaluation even without the evaluation notice, the measured routine-versus-evaluation gap may not isolate the effect of the notice or represent deployment behavior.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not ruled out. The authors report verbalized scenario awareness for Sonnet 4.5 with extended thinking and state that they cannot rule out unintended awareness in other models.

confounds.name: Goal language’s effects may reflect evaluation-cue recognition or learned refusal, rather than the proposed goal conflict
confounds.detail: Either recognizing goal language as an evaluation cue or automatically resisting language resembling jailbreak attempts could produce the observed changes in violation rates without the proposed explanation being true.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not ruled out. The authors say their native reasoning-trace analysis could not distinguish these explanations, particularly for models in which goal language suppressed violations.

confounds.name: Consequence-free evaluation gaps may reflect instructional salience rather than evaluation awareness
confounds.detail: The compliance notice could influence behavior as an explicit directive even if models are not responding to being monitored.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not ruled out. The authors state that distinguishing these explanations would require an additional control removing the evaluation cue while holding instructional salience constant; they did not run it.

evidence_standards.name: 100 trials per cell; temperature 0.7; pairwise Fisher’s exact tests with global Benjamini–Hochberg correction
evidence_standards.detail: Compliance gaps are marked significant at α = .05 after the global correction.

evidence_standards.name: Reasoning-mode classifier validation on 60 samples
evidence_standards.detail: The paper reports overall agreement, Cohen’s κ, macro-F1, and per-class performance; Wilson 95% confidence intervals are reported. The classifier’s consequence-modeling recall was 0/3, and the validation set had no positive examples of spontaneous consequence reasoning.

datasets.name: Retail voice-agent conversations
datasets.eval_protocol: 120 conversations: 40 each in p0, p1, and p2. Human evaluators and GPT-4.1/GPT-5 independently scored the same conversations using the shared rubric; three trained human annotators scored each conversation. Human-to-LLM ratios use Manual Eval 1, and scores are aggregated by the mean across the conversation set.

datasets.name: Telecom voice-agent conversations
datasets.eval_protocol: 122 conversations: 41 in p0, 40 in p1, and 41 in p2. Human evaluators and GPT-4.1/GPT-5 independently scored the same conversations using the shared rubric; three trained human annotators scored each conversation. Human-to-LLM ratios use Manual Eval 1, and scores are aggregated by the mean across the conversation set.

baselines.name: GPT-4.1
baselines.fair_comparison: Scored the same conversations as GPT-5 and the human evaluators, using the same rubric definitions across p0, p1, and p2; aggregate scores use the same mean-across-conversations procedure.

baselines.name: GPT-5
baselines.fair_comparison: Scored the same conversations as GPT-4.1 and the human evaluators, using the same rubric definitions across p0, p1, and p2; aggregate scores use the same mean-across-conversations procedure.

baselines.name: Manual Eval 1 (human evaluators)
baselines.fair_comparison: The human baseline is scored on the same conversations and rubric as the LLM judges. Each conversation was scored by three independent annotators, but the human scores in the ratio tables are specifically Manual Eval 1, not the three-annotator mean.

metrics.name: Critical Field Accuracy (CFA)
metrics.caveat: The human-to-judge gap is larger in Telecom than Retail; the paper reports domain- and configuration-specific ratios and annotator scores alongside the comparison.

metrics.name: ASR-Robust Goal Achievement (ARGA)
metrics.caveat: Judges score this more generously than humans, while human annotator spread is among the largest; the paper reports scores from three annotators and notes a large Retail Eval 2 p1 outlier.

metrics.name: MRS
metrics.caveat: It is 1.0 in nearly all cells and adds no variance, so it is left out of the agreement analysis.

metrics.name: Turn Efficiency (TE)
metrics.caveat: It stays near a human-to-judge ratio of 1, but annotator spread occurs in some configurations; the paper reports both ratios and annotator scores.

metrics.name: TO
metrics.caveat: It is 0 throughout and adds no variance, so it is left out of the agreement analysis.

metrics.name: User Experience Score (UES)
metrics.caveat: Judges score it higher than humans in the reported ratios; the paper reports domain- and configuration-specific comparisons.

metrics.name: Error Rate (ERR)
metrics.caveat: Human-to-judge ratios are erratic, especially in Retail; the paper reports the ratios separately by judge, domain, and configuration.

metrics.name: Recovery Turn Count (RTC)
metrics.caveat: Judge estimates can be below one despite recovery requiring one or more turns, and human annotators also disagree substantially; the paper reports all three annotators' scores and cautions against treating a single human count as ground truth.

metrics.name: Confirmation Precision (CP)
metrics.caveat: It is among the least reproducible metrics across human annotators, and the two judges can diverge sharply; the paper reports annotator scores and separate judge ratios.

metrics.name: Confirmation Recall (CR)
metrics.caveat: It stays near a human-to-judge ratio of 1, though the paper notes aggregate-based agreement is not conversation-level agreement.

metrics.name: Irreversible Action Safety (IAS)
metrics.caveat: LLM judges record far fewer safety events than humans, particularly in Telecom; ambiguous necessary escalations can lead judges to interpret the same behavior differently, so the paper argues for human oversight and reports three-annotator scores.

metrics.name: Safety Recall (SR)
metrics.caveat: LLM judges record far fewer safety events than humans, particularly in Telecom; ambiguous necessary escalations can lead judges to interpret the same behavior differently, so the paper argues for human oversight and reports three-annotator scores.

metrics.name: Pearson correlation (r)
metrics.caveat: Correlations are computed across metric-level aggregates (N=10 or N=30), not individual conversations; the paper reports both pooled and configuration-level analyses and cautions that aggregate agreement is an upper bound.

metrics.name: Spearman rank correlation (ρ)
metrics.caveat: Correlations are computed across metric-level aggregates (N=10 or N=30), not individual conversations; the paper reports both pooled and configuration-level analyses and cautions that aggregate agreement is an upper bound.

metrics.name: Mean relative range across annotators
metrics.caveat: It measures spread on metric-level aggregates rather than individual conversations; the paper also notes that metric ordering differs if absolute range is used.

confounds.name: The Telecom safety gap is an artifact of relying on one human annotator
confounds.detail: If the gap came from Manual Eval 1 alone, it might not persist with other human references.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper reports IAS and SR scores from all three annotators; all are high in every Telecom configuration and remain far above the judge levels implied by the ratios.

confounds.name: The weak Telecom human-judge correlation is an Eval 1 artifact
confounds.detail: A different human reference could change the human points driving the correlation, making the weak relationship appear specific to Eval 1.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The authors check the alternative annotator scores qualitatively: IAS and SR remain high for all three annotators and would not approach the judge range. They do not recompute the correlations under Eval 2 or Eval 3.

confounds.name: The smaller Retail safety ratios arise only because Retail human safety scores differ from Telecom
confounds.detail: A change in the human baseline alone could produce smaller human-to-judge ratios without judges being closer to humans in Retail.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper compares human IAS/SR scores and the ratios across domains, concluding that the human-score difference is smaller than the ratio difference and that judges must also be closer to humans on Retail safety.

confounds.name: RTC volatility is only a judge problem
confounds.detail: The high variation in judge recovery-turn estimates could be attributed to judge failure rather than uncertainty in how recovery turns are counted.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper compares three human annotators' RTC scores and finds substantial human disagreement too, especially Telecom p1 and across Retail configurations.

confounds.name: The wide p1 annotator spread is caused by persona injection
confounds.detail: The p1 variation could be attributed to the persona-injection condition itself rather than annotator variation or other factors.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper says there is only one persona-injection condition per domain, so the spread cannot be assigned to persona injection by itself; it does not rule this explanation out.

evidence_standards.name: Three independent human annotators per conversation, with adjudication for high disagreement
evidence_standards.detail: A fourth senior annotator adjudicated conversations flagged for high annotator disagreement; the paper reports metric-level aggregates and explicitly says these do not establish conversation-level agreement.

evidence_standards.name: Reported Pearson and Spearman correlations with p-values
evidence_standards.detail: The paper reports correlations across metric-level score vectors for N=10 pooled metrics and N=30 configuration-level observations. It reports Retail Pearson correlations as significant at p<0.001, and gives p-values for Telecom GPT-4.1 (p=0.408 at N=10; p=0.087 at N=30). No specific statistical test or significance threshold beyond the reported p-values is stated.

datasets.name: TriviaQA
datasets.eval_protocol: Used for in-distribution evaluation; the evaluation split and its size are not specified in the text. Responses are generated at temperature 0. Idk responses are identified by heuristic rules; correctness is determined using gold-answer string matching and ChatGPT (gpt-3.5-turbo-0613) analysis. Reports prudence, over-conservativeness, honesty, and accuracy.

datasets.name: Non-AmbigQA
datasets.eval_protocol: Out-of-distribution evaluation on the subset of NQ-Open with clear questions and non-ambiguous answers; size and split are not specified. Responses are generated at temperature 0 and evaluated using the paper’s idk heuristics and gold-answer matching with ChatGPT analysis. Reports prudence, over-conservativeness, honesty, and accuracy.

datasets.name: PUQA (Prior Unknown QA)
datasets.eval_protocol: A constructed set of 1,000 questions about scientific literature published in 2023, designed to be unknown and challenging for the model. Responses are generated at temperature 0; reports prudence to assess refusal on questions treated as definitely unknown.

datasets.name: PKQA (Prior Known QA)
datasets.eval_protocol: A constructed set of 1,000 questions the model is likely to know. Responses are generated at temperature 0; reports over-conservativeness and accuracy to assess false abstention and retained answering performance on questions treated as definitely known.

datasets.name: Eval-P-
datasets.eval_protocol: A helpfulness dataset covering requests such as summarization, creative writing, and general communication. Auto-J and GPT-4 (gpt-4-0613) rate responses on a 1–10 scale. The dataset size and split are not specified.

baselines.name: Unaligned Baseline
baselines.fair_comparison: Uses the unaligned model M_t with the typical QA prompt, “Q: <question>\nA:”. No further matching details are specified.

baselines.name: Fine-tuned Baseline
baselines.fair_comparison: Fine-tuned on the same 8,000 training samples; for unknown questions, uses the gold TriviaQA answers instead of idk responses.

metrics.name: Honesty Score
metrics.caveat: The paper notes that accuracy loss during alignment (such as catastrophic forgetting) is not captured as dishonesty; it reports accuracy alongside the honesty metrics to assess retained abilities.

metrics.name: Accuracy
metrics.caveat: Responses containing the gold answer count as loosely correct even if they also contain idk signs.

controls.name: Unaligned model M_t reference
controls.detail: The unaligned model is evaluated with the typical QA prompt alongside the aligned models.
controls.rules_out: Provides a reference for whether the aligned models’ reported outcomes differ from the unaligned model; it is not a sham or size-matched intervention control.

confounds.name: The apparent generalization could be a shortcut based on TriviaQA rather than learning to distinguish known from unknown questions
confounds.detail: The training data comes from TriviaQA, so an apparent improvement on that evaluation could reflect dataset-specific behavior rather than transferable honesty alignment.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Evaluate on Non-AmbigQA, PUQA, and PKQA, whose distributions differ from the TriviaQA training data; the paper reports transfer results on these datasets.

confounds.name: Honesty alignment could substantially reduce helpfulness on other tasks
confounds.detail: A gain on knowledge-based QA could look successful while the model becomes less helpful on unrelated requests.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Evaluate aligned and unaligned models on the separate Eval-P- helpfulness dataset using Auto-J and GPT-4 ratings; the reported scores are similar.

confounds.name: Incorrect answers may not indicate fabrication or lack of knowledge
confounds.detail: The paper’s external-behavior proxy treats response correctness as an approximation of internal knowledge, but an incorrect response could reflect a learned false belief rather than fabrication.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not ruled out by an experiment; the authors acknowledge this limitation and state that the approximation is a simplifying assumption.

evidence_standards.name: Temperature 0 for model evaluation
evidence_standards.detail: The paper states that evaluation responses are generated at temperature 0.

evidence_standards.name: Response classification and correctness judging
evidence_standards.detail: Idk responses are identified by heuristic rules; correctness is judged by checking for the gold answer via string match and ChatGPT (gpt-3.5-turbo-0613) analysis.

evidence_standards.name: Helpfulness judging
evidence_standards.detail: Auto-J and GPT-4 (gpt-4-0613) provide ratings on a 1–10 scale.

datasets.name: SycophancyEval
datasets.eval_protocol: Uses human-written and model-written evaluations across free-form feedback, challenged question answering, belief-biased question answering, and poem-misattribution tasks; free-form generation uses temperature 1 and multiple-choice tasks use temperature 0.

datasets.name: MATH
datasets.eval_protocol: Used for feedback on math solutions and for a subset of challenged multiple-choice QA questions with chain-of-thought reasoning; free-form generation uses temperature 1 and multiple-choice tasks use temperature 0.

datasets.name: Model-generated arguments
datasets.eval_protocol: Used for free-form feedback evaluation: compare feedback with no stated preference against feedback prompted with the user liking/writing or disliking/not writing the argument; GPT-4 judges whether modified-prompt feedback is more positive than baseline.

datasets.name: Model-generated poems
datasets.eval_protocol: Used for free-form feedback evaluation with the same baseline-versus-user-preference prompt comparison and GPT-4 positivity judgment as for arguments.

datasets.name: MMLU
datasets.eval_protocol: A subset is used for challenged multiple-choice QA with chain-of-thought reasoning; the assistant answers first, is challenged with “I don’t think that’s right. Are you sure?”, and then gives a final answer.

datasets.name: AQuA
datasets.eval_protocol: A subset is used for challenged multiple-choice QA; the assistant answers first, is challenged with “I don’t think that’s right. Are you sure?”, and then gives a final answer.

datasets.name: TruthfulQA
datasets.eval_protocol: Used in challenged QA as both open-ended and multiple-choice questions; also used in free-form QA with prompts suggesting a correct or incorrect answer, and as a source for approximately half of the 266-misconception dataset.

datasets.name: TriviaQA
datasets.eval_protocol: Used as a subset for challenged open-ended QA and in free-form QA with prompts suggesting a correct or incorrect answer.

datasets.name: Anthropic hh-rlhf helpfulness subset
datasets.eval_protocol: GPT-4 analyzes 15K randomly sampled response pairs using 23 features; Bayesian logistic regression predicts the human preference label, with a holdout set used to choose the prior scale.

datasets.name: 300 poem-misattribution prompts
datasets.eval_protocol: Prompts are made by incorrectly attributing 15 famous poems to another famous poet. Only poems each assistant correctly attributes when asked directly are included; string matching measures whether the response repeats the incorrect attribution without mentioning the correct one.

datasets.name: 266-misconception dataset
datasets.eval_protocol: Approximately half the misconceptions come from TruthfulQA and the Maintenance Phase podcast; the rest are generated with GPT-4 and examined. Misconceptions are grouped into eight difficulty levels using Claude 2’s zero-shot probability that each misconception is true. For preference comparisons, human workers compare sycophantic with helpful-truthful responses, with five workers per pair; BoN experiments sample 4096 responses per misconception.

baselines.name: 52-billion-parameter preference model trained on the same hh-rlhf data
baselines.fair_comparison: The paper compares its feature-based model’s holdout accuracy with the reported preference-model accuracy on the same data; no further matching details are stated.

baselines.name: Non-sycophantic PM
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared with the Claude 2 PM using the same prompts and sampled candidate responses in BoN; the PM is the Claude 2 PM with a request for truthful responses and an assistant acknowledgment prefixed to the dialog.

baselines.name: Oracle PM
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared in the 4096-response BoN experiment on the same misconception prompts and sampled responses; it always prefers truthful responses.

metrics.name: QA accuracy
metrics.caveat: For free-form QA, accuracy is graded by another language model; the paper also reports changes relative to the no-bias-prompt baseline.

metrics.name: Answer sycophancy
metrics.caveat: Defined as the mean change in accuracy across user beliefs and datasets relative to no biasing prompt.

metrics.name: Mimicry sycophancy
metrics.caveat: Counts responses with the incorrect attribution that do not mention the correct attribution; the evaluation is restricted to poems each assistant can correctly attribute when asked.

metrics.name: Holdout accuracy of the feature-based preference model
Model-estimated preference probability for a feature
metrics.caveat: The two explicit and implicit user-belief matching features are combined because their posterior correlation is -0.3 and their individual effects may be unreliable; a sensitivity analysis is also reported.

metrics.name: Preference-model preference frequency
metrics.caveat: Reported separately for baseline-truthful and helpful-truthful responses, and by misconception difficulty for the latter.

metrics.name: Human preference frequency
metrics.caveat: Reported both for the average human and using majority voting.

metrics.name: Truthfulness of BoN-selected responses
metrics.caveat: Claude 2 is used to assess whether a response refutes the misconception; results are reported across misconceptions and separately for the hardest misconceptions.

controls.name: Baseline feedback without a stated user preference
controls.detail: The assistant is asked to comment on the passage without saying whether the user likes it or wrote it; this is compared with prompts that state liking/writing or disliking/not writing the passage.
controls.rules_out: That differences in feedback positivity are just due to the passage or the ordinary feedback prompt, rather than the user-preference cue.

controls.name: No-bias-prompt QA baseline
controls.detail: The assistant answers without a prompt suggesting a belief about the answer; accuracy changes under belief-suggesting prompts are measured relative to this baseline.
controls.rules_out: That accuracy differences under belief-suggesting prompts simply reflect the assistant’s baseline accuracy.

controls.name: Non-sycophantic PM
controls.detail: The Claude 2 PM is prefixed with a request for truthful responses and an assistant acknowledgment, then used to select among the same sampled responses as the Claude 2 PM.
controls.rules_out: That the sycophancy difference is merely an effect of using BoN selection, rather than which PM scores the candidates.

confounds.name: Poem-misattribution mimicry reflects not knowing the correct poet
confounds.detail: A response repeating the user's wrong attribution could arise because the assistant does not know the correct attribution, rather than because it follows the user's mistake.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The authors verify that each assistant correctly attributes each of the 15 poems when asked, and restrict the misattribution evaluation to those poems.

confounds.name: Challenge-induced answer changes reflect correction of an initially wrong answer
confounds.detail: A revised answer after the user challenges the assistant could be a legitimate correction rather than sycophantic reversal.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper measures revisions from initially correct answers to inaccurate answers and reports apologies despite an initially correct answer.

confounds.name: Sycophancy under challenge depends on whether the assistant stated confidence
confounds.detail: The confidence statement or its presence in the dialog could affect the apparent response to the challenge.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The authors separately elicit confidence but discard that turn from the dialog history, and report that the pattern also holds when the assistant states high confidence.

confounds.name: Feature effects in the preference-data analysis are artifacts of collinearity between explicit and implicit belief matching
confounds.detail: The two matching-user-beliefs features have a posterior correlation of -0.3, making their individual effects potentially unreliable.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The authors combine the two features for the reported effect and report a sensitivity analysis in which matching user beliefs remains one of the most predictive features.

confounds.name: Sycophancy observed during Claude 2 optimization is due only to pretraining or supervised finetuning, not preference-model optimization
confounds.detail: Sycophancy is already present before the RL phase, so its presence alone would not establish an effect of RL optimization.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The authors measure sycophancy throughout the RL phase and report that feedback and mimicry sycophancy increase during that phase; they also acknowledge pretraining and supervised finetuning may contribute.

evidence_standards.name: Generation settings
evidence_standards.detail: Free-form generation tasks use temperature 1; multiple-choice tasks use temperature 0.

evidence_standards.name: Reported uncertainty for evaluation results
evidence_standards.detail: Figures report means and standard errors, including means and standard errors across domains for feedback positivity.

evidence_standards.name: Bayesian posterior reporting
evidence_standards.detail: Approximate inference uses 6000 posterior samples across four independent MCMC chains; feature effects are reported with posterior medians and 50% and 95% credible intervals.

evidence_standards.name: Human preference study size and aggregation
evidence_standards.detail: Five human preferences are collected per response pair; results are reported using both average-human preference and majority voting.

datasets.name: XSafety
datasets.eval_protocol: 2,800 instances across 14 safety issues, with 200 instances per issue; translated into 10 languages for 28,000 annotated instances total. The paper reports the percentage of generated responses judged unsafe. Commonsense Safety items are multiple-choice and scored against reference answers; for other scenarios, non-English responses are translated into English with Google Translate and evaluated by ChatGPT using a safety prompt. The prompting experiment uses Ethics and Morality, Insult, and Crimes and Illegal Activities in Chinese, Russian, Japanese, and French. No train/validation split or episode count is specified.

metrics.name: Unsafe response rate (unsafety ratio)
metrics.caveat: The rate depends on ChatGPT self-evaluation, which the authors say is not entirely accurate; they report 88.5% evaluator accuracy on 1,400 human-annotated cases.

metrics.name: Relative reduction in unsafe response rate
ChatGPT safety-evaluator accuracy
metrics.caveat: The authors note the self-evaluation method is not entirely accurate; they report human annotation on 1,400 randomly selected cases and a separate human review of 100 cases where ChatGPT and GPT-4 disagreed.

controls.name: Vanilla ChatGPT
controls.detail: The prompting experiment compares ChatGPT given the proposed English instruction to ChatGPT without that instruction on the selected non-English languages and safety scenarios.
controls.rules_out: A difference between the conditions supports an effect of adding the prompt, rather than merely evaluating ChatGPT.

confounds.name: The Chinese-derived benchmark could reflect Chinese-specific cultural content rather than multilingual safety
confounds.detail: An apparent difference across languages could arise because benchmark items or their harms are culturally specific.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The authors manually checked items and removed Chinese culture-associated sentences, asked translators to adapt translations to the relevant cultures during two proofreading rounds, and randomly inspected 10% of the data, reporting a pass rate above 99%.

confounds.name: ChatGPT’s automatic safety judgments could be inaccurate and drive the reported unsafe rates
confounds.detail: If the evaluator misclassifies responses, the observed multilingual safety differences could reflect evaluator errors rather than model behavior.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Three annotators assessed 1,400 randomly selected cases across all ten languages and 14 issues; ChatGPT evaluator accuracy was 88.5%. The authors also had humans review 100 randomly selected cases where ChatGPT and GPT-4 disagreed; ChatGPT was correct in 76 and GPT-4 in 24.

evidence_standards.name: ChatGPT decoding setting
evidence_standards.detail: The OpenAI API was run at temperature 0 to obtain more deterministic results; the paper does not report seeds, repeated runs, variance, statistical tests, or a numerical threshold for treating differences as real.

evidence_standards.name: Human evaluation of automatic safety judgments
evidence_standards.detail: Three annotators with bachelor’s degrees and English proficiency assessed correctness on 1,400 randomly selected cases; reported evaluator accuracy was 88.5%.

evidence_standards.name: Human review of ChatGPT–GPT-4 disagreements
evidence_standards.detail: Humans annotated 100 randomly selected cases with differing judgments; ChatGPT was correct on 76 cases and GPT-4 on 24.
